newsitem.title: UK: European bonds will outmanoeuvre U.S., charts say.
newsitem.headline: European bonds will outmanoeuvre U.S., charts say.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
One day after U.S. Treasury-bond futures tumbled nearly two full points, their European counterparts were racking up chunky gains on Monday.
Technical analysts called the divergence unusual, but said it might continue in the near term, particularly at the short end, as European bonds chase new highs on the charts.
"I don't see any major decoupling but I think we are certainly looking for Europe to continue to outperform," said Richard Adcock, manager of technical research at HSBC Futures in London.

Treasuries were knocked flat on Friday by U.S. jobs growth in December well above analyst expectations. The U.S. Labor Department said 262,000 jobs had been added to the non-farm sector. Economists had expected growth of around 200,000.
The data sent March T-bond futures skidding to a low of 109-26 from a high of 111-21 as expectations rose that the U.S. Federal Reserve would have to raise rates to snuff out potential inflation.
Eurodollars, which give a picture of market expectations of interest rate movement, also suffered, with the March contract losing 12 basis points and the June contract 15 basis points.

European contracts certainly felt the pain, but not to the same extent. By Monday they were bouncing higher, with Spanish bond futures and Italian setting a new record highs, and German, French and British futures all up markedly.
HSBC's Adcock said European markets had breached important technical resistance on Monday, setting the stage for further gains in the short term.

March German Bunds on LIFFE cracked 100.41, a down trendline connecting recent highs and zoomed through an old gap. March British gilts pierced trendline resistance at 109-17 before falling back and March French notionnel futures pushed past 129.00 level.
By 1516 GMT, Bunds were up 0.77 at 100.84, gilts were up 15/32 at 109-14 and notionnel were up 1.00 at 129.70. Italian BTPs were 1.40 higher at 130.18, setting new all-time highs.
"The overall picture still looks pretty constructive for Europe and tends to suggest that we will see the strength being extended, possibly to challenge contract highs at some point," Adcock said.
Meanwhile, March T-bond futures in Chicago had further to fall, technical analysts said. T-bonds were up 5/32 at 110-16.

Tom Hobson, director of technical analysis at Merrill Lynch in London, said T-bonds may nudge a little higher to 111-00 but would then drop back to test the 109-22 area, a 61.8 percent retracement of the 11-point rally from September to December.
Hobson said, however, the biggest divergence in European and U.S. bond markets on charts would come at the short end, where economists expect interest rates in Europe to hold steady or even fall.
"The European short ends are extremely positive," he said. "We had break-outs above month-long resistance last week, particularly in Euromark and Pibor."

June Euromark futures broke above resistance around 96.86 last Wednesday and were quoted at 96.90 on Monday, up 0.03 on the day. March Pibor futures pushed through 96.73 resistance. On Monday they were at 96.81, up 0.03 on the day.
In the back months, the split is even more pronounced, Hobson said, with March 1998 Euromarks outperforming March 1998 Eurodollars by 90 basis points in the last six weeks.
"That's a little bit difficult to sustain in the short term," he said.
Further out, European bonds would be susceptible to a U.S. downturn, analysts said.
"I don't think they can move around independently for very long," said David Wood, independent technical analyst near London. "If one goes a long way down, the other has to drift lower."
